full_judgment:
75. As per the Chambers Dictionary, 10th edition "appear" means "to become visible; to present oneself formally before an authority, court, etc; to act as the legal representative or counsel for another; to come into view (emphasis supplied), to come before the public; to perform (on stage or on film, etc); to be published; to be manifest ; to seem ." In New Oxford Advanced Learners Dictionary as many as 8 (eight) meanings have been shown against the word "appear" and of these 8 meanings, meaning No.1 is relevant in the context. Meaning 1.appear means "LOOK/SEEM (emphasis supplied) linking verb (not used in the progressive tenses) to give the impression of being (emphasis supplied) or doing sth, SEEM : [VADJ] She did not appear at all surprised at the news [V-N]. He appears a perfectly normal person [v to inf )She appeared to be in her late thirties(emphasis supplied). They appeared not to know what was happening. There appears to have been a mistake [v (that) it appears that there has been a mistake. It appears unlikely that interest rates will fall further. It would appear that this was a major problem.]" It is also the golden rule of construction that all statutes are to be construed according to the plain, literal and grammatical meaning of the words and when words in a statute are clear and unambiguous they should be construed according to their tenor and meaning for that reflects the intent and purpose of a legislation; the court to construe a provision of a statute according to the ordinary and natural meaning of the language used by the legislature as the language so supplied best declares the intention of the legislature and recourse to any other principle of interpretation is unnecessary. The language used in sub-section (1) of section 66 is very plain, simple, clear and unambiguous. Keeping in view the dictionary meaning of the word "appear" and from a reading of the words "and it appears to the court that he is a child(emphasis supplied)" used in subsection (1) of section 66, it prima facie appears to us that the legislature has given a plenary jurisdiction or power to the Court to take a first hand decision by way of presumption/assumption/ formation of opinion as to the age of a person, whether charged with an offence or not, whenever is brought before it otherwise than for the purpose of giving evidence whether he is a child and then to make an inquiry in that respect as mandated in the section itself. Reading the sub-section in its entirety, it also appears to us that to take recourse to the process of inquiry as to the age of the person so brought before a court and record a finding stating his age, it is a precondition that the Court must first presume/assume/form an opinion that the person so brought is a child. 

 76. The Act, 1974 is a special law and various benefits have been given in the Act to a child offender which are not available to an adult offender, so to give those benefits to a child offender, the Court before whom a person is brought, must presume/assume/form opinion first as to his/her age and if it appears to it that he/she is a child and then on inquiry as mandated in section 66(1) if it is determined that he is really under the age of 16, then and then only he/she would be given the benefits of the Act. There is a good logic behind such scheme by the legislature. The reason, as we could see, is that there may be divergent types of cases which may come before a Court. There may be cases when admittedly in the FIR or in the petition of complaint as the case may be or in the charge-sheet and may be in a confessional statement made by such person, the age has uniformally been written or mentioned under 16, i.e. may be 14 years, 15 years or just under 16years and such mentioning of age is not disputed by the prosecution or the private party concerned, then no presumption /assumption/formation of a first hand idea as to whether the person is a child or not would be needed or called for. There may be cases when the age of the person so brought is mentioned in the above mentioned documents as 16 or any other approximate age (but not under 16) or even above, there may be cases where no age is mentioned and the person so brought claims to be a child by filing documents, but the prosecution or the state or the private party concerned opposes the claim of the person to be a child claiming that he/she is adult, i.e. above 16 or high. There may be cases where the age of a person is exaggeratively mentioned by the complaining party or the law enforcing agencies to show him adult, but in fact, he is under the age of 16, yet there may be a case where only in one document, such as, the confessional statement made by a per- son under section 164 of the Code, as happened in the instant case, in the confessional statements of appellant Asha recorded by the Magistrate, First Class, his age was mentioned 16, but the Sessions Judge found him major and above 18 along with two other appellants and in all these cases, the Court first has to assume/presume/form a first hand idea that the person so brought is a child and, then and then, only it would be obligatory upon it to make an inquiry as to the age of that person in the manner as stated in section 66( 1) of the Act, 1974 and record a finding stating his age as nearly as may be (emphasis supplied). If it is interpreted that whenever any person, whether charged with an offence or not, is brought before any criminal Court and he claims to be under the age of 16 on the date of occurrence or on a particular date may be on the date of framing of charge "then it must be accepted that on that date he could have been below 16 and not above 16" as opined in the separate opinion by learned brother, Muhammad Imman Ali, J, though actually, the person apparently appears to be above 16 and much more high age as in the instant case, then the Court before whom such person is brought shall have no option but to go for inquiry to determine his/her age as mandated in the section, in that case the Court shall be stripped of the plenary power/jurisdiction given to it by the legislature to presume/ assume/form its first hand opinion whether that person is a child or not and in the process, the first part of the section shall become meaningless or redundant. But the provisions of a statute cannot be interpreted in such a way that renders any part thereof meaningless or redundant. Moreso, interpretation of a statute cannot be such that nugates the power given to a Court by the legislature and giving such interpretation, we shall be questioning the wisdom of the legislature. We must also keep in mind another cardinal principle of construction that the legislature never uses any word unnecessary or without any meaning or purpose and no word in a statute should be treated as surplus or redundant and a construction which would render any part of the language of a statute without any effect will normally be rejected. 

 77. Presumption/assumption/formation of opinion by the Court whether the person brought before it is a child or not, as envisaged in sub-section (1) of section 66, may be from his physical appearance (as was presumed in the instant case) or with reference to papers and documents produced by the parties concerned and may be in consideration of both. And to presume/assume/form such a first hand idea by a Court, it need not be a doctor or a medical expert and no radiological or bone ossification report is necessary. It is also significant to note that even after inquiry the Court shall record a finding as to the age of the person so brought "as nearly as may be." 

 and as discussed above, the learned Sessions Judge was quite authorized under section 66(1) of the Act, 1974 to hold such presumption/assumption/ formation of his opinion as to the age of the appellants. So, there was no scope of appearance to the Sessions Judge that the appellants were under the age of 16 years and, as such, the question of making an enquiry as to their age within the meaning of section 66(1) did not arise at all. It is also to be noted that in reply to the charges brought against them, none of the appellants (including Asha), at all, claimed that they were children. For the same reason, the learned Sessions Judge did not accept the papers such as registration cards of Secondary School Certificate of appellants, Modern and Asha and the affidavits sworn by the parents of the appellants which were filed during their examinations under section 342 of the Code in a bid to show that they were under the age of 16 years. The High Court Division also on consideration of the age of the appellants as mentioned in the FIR, in their confessional statements and in their examinations under section 342 of the Code, gave specific finding that: "From evidence produced and materials placed before court below it is manifestly clear that convict appellants were neither had been child nor juvenile within the meaning of Children's Act during course of commission of felony and also framing of charge. They stand proved to be major or adult at the time of commission of offence and, also, framing of charge." 

 "66. Presumption and determination of age.-(1) Whenever a person whether charged with an offence or not, is brought before any criminal Court otherwise than for the purpose of giving evidence, and it appears to the Court that he is a child, the Court shall make an inquiry as to the age of that person and, for that purpose, shall take such evidence as may be forthcoming at the hearing of the case, and shall record a finding thereon, stating his age as nearly as may be."
